shower.thought: We measure our lives in years, but we experience them in moments—so someone who has fewer years but more moments might have lived longer than someone who lived decades on autopilot.
If you've ever forgotten a traumatic event, how do you know it shaped you? You're living with the consequences of something you don't remember.
The saddest part about growing up isn't losing wonder—it's realizing that other people lost theirs too, and nobody talks about it.
You can't think of nothing. Even when you try to clear your mind, you're aware that you're trying, which is itself a thought.
We assume silence is peaceful, but silence is just sound we've decided to ignore. The noise was always there.
Every conversation you have slightly changes who you are, which means everyone you meet is technically altering your existence without your permission.
The things you're most ashamed of are probably the things you have most in common with everyone else—but nobody says them out loud, so you feel alone.
You're terrified of being forgotten, but you'll never actually know if you are, because you won't exist to experience it.
The reason we love stories is because they have endings. Real life is just a story that keeps going, which is why it feels less meaningful.
You've only ever lived one day at a time, but somehow you're 30 or 40 or 50 years old. The daily you and the yearly you are practically different people.
If a tree falls in a forest with no one around, it makes a sound. But if you forget something happened, did it really happen to you?
We call it "falling asleep" like it's passive, but you're actually performing an act of faith—trusting that you'll wake up the same person.
Most of your memories are probably false, containing details added, changed, or imagined. Your past is fiction you believe in.
The people you loved ten years ago still exist somewhere, but the version of them you loved doesn't. You're mourning someone who's still alive.
You'll never see your own face naturally—only in reflections or photos. You're the only person who knows what you look like secondhand.
Procrastination isn't laziness; it's hope. You believe future-you will be different, smarter, or more capable than present-you. You're always disappointed.
The more you understand how something works, the less magical it becomes. Knowledge might just be the slow erasure of wonder.
We're taught to be ourselves, but "yourself" is just a character you've been rehearsing so long, you forgot it was a performance.
If aliens visited Earth, the first thing we'd do is explain human behavior to them. We'd finally have to answer the question: what are we actually doing here?
You spend 16 hours a day awake, but your brain is only truly conscious for maybe two of them. What's it doing the rest of the time?

Your limitations are only as real as you believe them to be. — Unknown
Progress is not about perfection. It's about direction. — Unknown
The obstacle is the way. — Marcus Aurelius
Most of life's failures are people who did not realize how close they were to success when they gave up. — Thomas Edison
Discipline is choosing between what you want now and what you want most. — Unknown
You cannot control the wind, but you can adjust your sails. — Dolly Parton
The difference between who you are and who you want to be is what you do. — Unknown
Regret for the things we did is temporary; regret for the things we did not do is permanent. — Sydney Harris
Small daily improvements are the key to staggering long-term results. — Robin Sharma
Your potential is endless. Your excuses are not. — Unknown
The only permission you need is your own. — Unknown
Courage is not the absence of fear. It is moving forward despite it. — Unknown

darkjoke.thought:
I told my wife she was drawing her eyebrows too high.
She looked surprised.

My gym trainer said I'd never get in shape if I kept making excuses.
I said, "You're right—I'm switching to a new trainer."
I have a stepladder because my real ladder left when I was just a kid.

People ask me how I stay so calm during stressful situations.
I tell them it's because I stopped caring about anything that matters.

My doctor asked if there's any history of mental illness in my family.
I said, "Does it count if I'm creating the history right now?"

I was worried about my friend's drinking, so I asked if he wanted to talk about it.
He said, "Not really," and we haven't spoken in six months.

My girlfriend asked why I never remember our anniversary.
I said, "Because if I remembered it, you'd know I was capable of remembering things."
I wanted to make a joke about my dead grandmother, but I figured she'd already heard it.

My therapist told me I use humor as a defense mechanism.
I said, "That's ridiculous," and we both laughed until she billed me for the extra time.

At my uncle's funeral, my aunt kept saying he was "in a better place now."
I wanted to ask which funeral home, but the timing felt off.

I told my friend he needed to be more optimistic.
He said, "Why? So I can be disappointed in high definition?"
My life is like a movie—if the movie was three hours long and nothing happened.

I asked my accountant if there was any way to reduce my tax burden.
He said, "Have you considered not making any money?"

People keep asking me what my five-year plan is.
I don't know—I can barely commit to a streaming service.

My mother-in-law asked when we were having kids.
I said, "When you move out," and now we're legally required to go to family therapy.
I'm not saying my childhood was rough, but my imaginary friend filed a restraining order.

My dating profile says I'm fluent in sarcasm.
Turns out that's not as attractive as I thought.

I told my boss I'd been with the company for ten years and deserved recognition.
He said, "You're right—I finally know your name."

My friend said he was going through a rough patch.
I offered to listen, but apparently that just means I'm "enabling his negative spiral."

I asked a girl for her number at the gym.
She said she was married, and I said, "So was I—that's not what stopped me."
